transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Korva Coleman.
There was a flight disturbance today on a commercial jet belonging to Fly Dubai.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says one pilot tried to stab another one.
The Israeli leader says he then tried to crash the plane.
Many passengers aboard are Israeli.
The plane diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia.
The pilot and co-pilot have been hospitalized.
Stocks opened higher this morning as the Commerce Department delivered a cooler than expected.
Inflation report.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones industrial rose about 30 points in early trading.
Consumer prices in August were up 3.4 percent from a year ago, according to the Commerce
Department's inflation yardstick, which is closely washed by the Federal Reserve.
Gasoline and diesel prices inched lower overnight, but remained much higher than they were before
the U.S. launched its war with Iran.
The U.S. economy grew a bit faster this spring than first reported.
Some updated figures show GDP grew at an annual rate of 2.2 percent in April/May/June, thanks
to upward revisions to consumer and government spending and investment.
And President Trump's tariff policy is back in court today.
Importers in nearly two dozen states are challenging the latest round of import taxes as illegal.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Prosecutors in Massachusetts are still deciding whether Lindsay Clancy will be retried on
charges of killing her three young children.
At member station WBUR, Deborah Becker reports.
Judge William Sullivan took several motions under advisement filed by both sides and set
another hearing date for November.
Some motions asked the judge to dismiss the case.
Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz said his office is still considering whether
there will be a new trial.
There's no determination to me that's anything.
We're doing it.
We're doing it.
We're doing a due diligence.
We're going to continue to do that.
We'd say when he would decide or whether Clancy would be charged with first-degree murder
again or lesser charges.
For NPR News, I'm Deborah Becker in Boston.
A new poll looks at what voters in rural America think about President Trump's Make America
Healthy Again movement.
Sarah Jane Tribble with KFF Health News has more.
About eight in 10 rural voters said President Trump's health care policies have had a negative
effect or no impact on the health of people where they live, according to a new poll by
the Associated Press and KFF.
Kim Solis is a small business owner in Texas.
She says her health care costs have climbed since Trump returned to office, and she worries
about medical emergencies.
Certainly we'd be in a world of hurt trying to take money out of savings or getting it
out of our 401(k) just to be able to do something about it.
My brother-in-law for an example, he has to have a shoulder replacement and he can't even
afford it right now.
The poll surveyed more than 2,000 rural voters in mid-August.
That's Sarah Jane Tribble with KFF Health News.
You're listening to NPR.
President Trump says artificial intelligence companies can self-regulate their developments.
He held a meeting with dozens of AI industry leaders at the White House yesterday.
Trump says that some AI industry leaders signed a voluntary agreement he posted online, but
there are no details on how the big tech companies will agree to police problems.
North Korea has rejected accusations that it planted landmines in the demilitarized
zone separating the two Koreas.
Two mines exploded last week, injuring three South Korean soldiers.
NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports from Seoul.
The South calls this an attack on its forces.
The United Nations Command enforces the armistice that ended fighting in the Korean War in 1953.
In a statement, the UNC said that they conducted a joint investigation with the South Korean
military and found a live North Korean anti-personnel mine in the southern half of the DMZ in violation
of armistice agreements.
South Korea's military demanded an apology from the North and called on it to stop fortifying
positions within the DMZ.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's sister Kim Yo-jong called the South's findings a fabrication.
She said that the North has a right to fortify its border and its troops will retaliate if
fired upon.
Anthony Kuhn in PR News, Seoul.
In the U.S., forecasters say Hurricane Polo is broken up over northern Mexico, but its
heavy moisture is still streaming north.
There are flood watches and warnings posted from the desert southwest up to Illinois.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Pilot attempts to stab co-pilot and crash Fly Dubai commercial aircraft; plane diverts to Saudi Arabia
Stock market opens higher as Commerce Department reports inflation cooled to 3.4 percent in August
U.S. GDP growth revised upward to 2.2 percent annual rate for second quarter
Importers challenge Trump tariff policy in court across nearly two dozen states
Massachusetts prosecutors decide whether to retry Lindsay Clancy on charges of killing three children
Rural voters say Trump health care policies negatively impact their communities, poll finds
President Trump meets with AI industry leaders on voluntary self-regulation agreements
North Korea rejects accusations of planting landmines in demilitarized zone; two mines injured South Korean soldiers
Hurricane Polo breaks apart over northern Mexico; heavy moisture brings flood watches to southwest and Illinois
